opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think when people see Skild showing demos on both humanoids and quadrupeds, the natural reaction is "why are they spreading themselves across so many bodies?" But I read it the opposite way. To me it's a statement of their core bet: that the valuable thing isn't any single robot, it's the brain, a general foundation model that can sit on top of many different embodiments.

If you believe that, you *have* to show it working across very different hardware. A dog and a humanoid are almost opposite ends of the spectrum. A quadruped is statically more stable, its locomotion problem is relatively well understood, and the commercial use cases, like inspection or patrol, are already somewhat real. A humanoid is much harder: balance, whole-body control, manipulation with hands. If one model, or one training recipe, can transfer across both, that's a much stronger claim than "we made one robot do a cool trick."

There's also a data argument. Robotics is starved for data compared to language or vision. If you can pool experience across embodiments, simulation, teleoperation, maybe human video, then each new body isn't starting from zero. Cross-embodiment training is one of the few plausible ways to get anything like scaling laws in robotics.

That said, I'd stay a bit cautious. A demo across platforms doesn't necessarily mean a truly shared model doing the heavy lifting. Sometimes it's a shared framework with a lot of per-robot tuning underneath. The real test is how quickly they can bring up a brand-new robot they've never seen, with how little new data, and how robust it is outside curated environments. Locomotion transfer is one thing; dexterous manipulation transferring across bodies is much harder, and that's where most of the economic value will eventually be.

So my interpretation: strategically it makes sense, it's the "be the Android, not the phone maker" play. Whether the technology is fully there yet is something we'll only know as they deploy in messy, real-world settings rather than in videos.

r001.rationale: The response says quadruped commercial use cases are somewhat real, but does not suggest Skild needs robot mobility because it is approaching commercial deployment.

r002.rationale: It explains the work as a bet on a general model that transfers across embodiments, not as a response to mobility needs.

fable-5.1.text:
Skild. Yeah, I think people sometimes look at that and ask, so are they a humanoid company, or a quadruped company, or what? And I'd say that question kind of misses what they're actually trying to do.

The way I read it, the humanoid and the dog are not the product. They're the two form factors that are most available to buy right now, in decent quantities, from a bunch of different manufacturers. If your thesis is that you're building a general robot brain, a foundation model for control, then you need to prove it transfers across embodiments. So you take the cheapest, most diverse hardware you can get your hands on, and you show the same model driving a Unitree dog and a humanoid with different kinematics and different sensors. The dog is a great test case because it's cheap, it's robust, you can collect a lot of data and break a lot of them. The humanoid is the harder, more aspirational one. Having both lets you demonstrate the thing that actually matters to them, which is cross-embodiment generalization.

The second thing is just pragmatic. Those are the platforms with the most sim and real data behind them, so you can get reinforcement learning in simulation to transfer. Locomotion on legged robots is honestly one of the more mature areas, so it's a reasonable place to show results early while the manipulation side, which is much harder, catches up.

What I'd be cautious about is reading too much into demo videos. A dog walking over rubble or a humanoid getting up after a shove, those are impressive, but they're mostly locomotion. The real question for a company like that is whether the same approach gets you to reliable manipulation in cluttered environments. That's where the economic value is, and that's where I'd watch for evidence. Right now I'd say the hardware choices tell you more about their thesis of being hardware-agnostic than about any particular bet on humanoids winning.

If by dog-related robots you mean quadrupeds, those and humanoids pose different challenges in balance, movement, and interaction. Working on both could suggest an interest in broader robotic capabilities. But I’d be cautious about inferring a firm strategy from the apparent work alone.
